questions.question: What is AWS Lambda and how does it differ from EC2?
questions.answer: Lambda is a serverless compute service — you provide code and a trigger, AWS manages all the infrastructure. EC2 gives you a virtual machine you must provision, configure, patch, and manage. With Lambda, you pay per millisecond of execution; with EC2 you pay by the hour regardless of whether your code runs. Lambda scales automatically per invocation; EC2 requires manual or Auto Scaling configuration.

questions.question: What is a Lambda cold start and when does it occur?
questions.answer: A cold start is the initialization delay Lambda incurs when it must create a new execution container for a function that has no warm container available. It occurs on the first invocation after deployment, after a long period of inactivity, or when Lambda scales out to handle more concurrent requests than existing containers can serve. Cold starts add milliseconds to seconds of latency depending on runtime and package size.

questions.question: What is the maximum execution timeout for a Lambda function?
questions.answer: 15 minutes (900 seconds). The default timeout is 3 seconds. Lambda will forcibly terminate any function that runs longer than the configured timeout.

questions.question: What is an IAM execution role and why does every Lambda function need one?
questions.answer: An execution role is an IAM role that Lambda assumes during execution, giving the function temporary credentials to call other AWS services. Lambda functions have no inherent permissions — without an execution role that explicitly grants access, the function cannot read from S3, write to DynamoDB, publish to SNS, or interact with any other AWS service. Every Lambda function must have an execution role.

questions.question: What is DynamoDB Streams and how is it used in event-driven architectures?
questions.answer: DynamoDB Streams is a time-ordered log that captures item-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) in a DynamoDB table and makes them available for up to 24 hours. In event-driven architectures, Streams acts as a trigger — when a record changes, a connected Lambda function is automatically invoked with the change data as the event payload. This enables loose coupling: the service writing data doesn't need to know about the service reacting to it.

questions.question: What is Amazon SNS and what is the pub/sub model?
questions.answer: Amazon SNS is a fully managed publish/subscribe messaging service. In the pub/sub model, a publisher sends a message to a named topic without knowing who receives it. SNS then fans the message out simultaneously to all subscribers. Subscribers can be email addresses, SMS numbers, HTTP endpoints, SQS queues, Lambda functions, or mobile push endpoints. Adding or removing subscribers requires no changes to the publisher.

questions.question: Why must you confirm an SNS email subscription before receiving notifications?
questions.answer: SNS requires confirmation to prevent spam and unauthorized subscriptions. When you subscribe an email address, SNS sends a confirmation email. The subscription stays in 'PendingConfirmation' status until you click the confirmation link. SNS will not deliver any messages to an unconfirmed email subscription — it simply silently discards them.

questions.question: What S3 event type triggers a Lambda function when a file is uploaded?
questions.answer: s3:ObjectCreated:* covers all object creation events — PUT, POST, COPY, and multipart upload completions. You can be more specific (s3:ObjectCreated:Put) or use the wildcard to catch any creation method, which is what 'All object create events' selects in the console.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege and how does it apply to Lambda execution roles?
questions.answer: Least privilege means granting only the minimum permissions necessary for a task. For Lambda execution roles, this means not attaching broad managed policies like AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess when the function only needs dynamodb:PutItem on a specific table. In production, create custom IAM policies that specify exact actions (Effect: Allow, Action: dynamodb:PutItem) on exact resource ARNs (arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:ACCOUNT:table/Inventory) — nothing broader.

questions.question: What are S3 bucket name requirements?
questions.answer: S3 bucket names must be globally unique across all AWS accounts and regions worldwide, 3–63 characters long, lowercase only, can contain letters, numbers, and hyphens, must start and end with a letter or number, and cannot be formatted as an IP address. Common patterns to ensure uniqueness: include your account ID, use a timestamp, or add random digits.

questions.question: Situation: Your Lambda function processes inventory files from S3. After deploying a code fix, the function still behaves as before. What did you likely forget?
questions.answer: (Situation) Code change was made in the Lambda console editor but the behavior didn't update. (Task) Ensure the new code is actually running. (Action) Check whether the Deploy button was clicked after saving the code — in the Lambda console, changes are not live until you explicitly deploy them. Clicked Deploy, waited for the 'Changes deployed' confirmation banner. (Result) Function ran the updated code on next invocation. This is the single most common Lambda mistake according to Todd — 'one little button, that's all it takes.'

questions.question: Situation: You configure a Lambda function triggered by API Gateway. The function processes an AI model request. It works for short prompts but returns a 504 error for long prompts. Lambda logs show 31-second execution. What's wrong?
questions.answer: (Situation) Short prompts work; long prompts return 504. Lambda logs show successful 31-second execution. (Task) Identify why successful Lambda executions result in client-side errors. (Action) Investigated API Gateway timeout — API Gateway has a hard 29-second timeout that cannot be changed. Lambda completed at second 31, but API Gateway already closed the connection at second 29 and returned a 504 to the client. Lambda's own timeout setting is irrelevant here. (Result) Changed architecture — moved to async processing pattern, using SQS or Step Functions to decouple the API response from the long-running Lambda execution.

questions.question: Situation: You upload a CSV file to S3 but nothing appears in DynamoDB. How do you debug this?
questions.answer: (Situation) S3 upload complete, DynamoDB table empty after 30 seconds. (Task) Find why the Lambda didn't write data. (Action) Checked CloudWatch Logs for Load-Inventory function — looked for the most recent log stream. Common causes found: (1) Lambda was never invoked — indicates S3 event notification wasn't saved or Lambda permission for S3 to invoke it is missing; (2) Lambda was invoked but threw an exception — check the error message in logs; (3) DynamoDB access denied — execution role missing DynamoDB write permission. Used CloudWatch Log Insights to filter logs efficiently across multiple invocations. (Result) Resolved by correcting the IAM execution role to include DynamoDB write permissions.

questions.question: Situation: A student uploads 6 CSV files simultaneously and expects to receive 6 SNS email alerts. They only receive 3. What might be happening?
questions.answer: (Situation) 6 files uploaded, only 3 stores generated alerts. (Task) Determine why some stores didn't trigger alerts. (Action) Checked each CSV — realized 3 of the 6 stores (Springfield, Pusan, Berlin) each have one item with count=0, while Shanghai also has Amazon Tap at 0. Checked CloudWatch logs for Check-Stock to see which invocations ran. Possible causes: (1) DynamoDB trigger was newly enabled and not yet processing — waited 2–3 minutes; (2) SNS subscription still pending confirmation for some recipients; (3) Some files failed to parse due to encoding issues. (Result) After waiting for trigger propagation, all expected alerts arrived.

questions.question: Situation: A colleague asks why you didn't add stock-checking logic directly inside Load-Inventory instead of creating a second Lambda. How do you justify two functions?
questions.answer: (Situation) Architectural decision questioned — why two separate Lambdas? (Task) Explain the design rationale. (Action) Explained Single Responsibility Principle: Load-Inventory has one job (load data), Check-Stock has one job (check stock levels). Combining them would mean: (1) Load-Inventory failures also break notifications; (2) Notification logic bugs force redeployment of the data loading function; (3) Adding a third downstream process (e.g., auto-reorder) requires touching Load-Inventory instead of just adding a new subscriber to DynamoDB Streams. Decoupled functions are independently testable, independently scalable, and independently deployable. (Result) Colleague agreed — new notification features can be added as new Lambda subscribers without touching the data pipeline.

questions.question: Situation: Your Check-Stock Lambda keeps failing. CloudWatch shows it runs but you receive no email alerts. What are the first three things you check?
questions.answer: (Situation) Check-Stock Lambda invoked successfully per logs, but no emails received. (Task) Find why notifications aren't delivered. (Action) Checked three things in order: (1) SNS subscription status — went to SNS console, checked if subscription showed 'Confirmed' or 'PendingConfirmation'; the email needed re-confirmation. (2) Lambda execution role — verified Lambda-Check-Stock-Role has AmazonSNSFullAccess or sns:Publish permission on the NoStock topic. (3) Check-Stock logs for errors — looked for AccessDeniedException or incorrect topic ARN matching. Found the subscription was unconfirmed. (Result) Confirmed subscription, received alerts immediately on next test upload.

questions.question: Situation: You need to deploy the same serverless inventory system in three environments: dev, staging, prod — each pointing to different DynamoDB tables and SNS topics. How do you handle this without duplicating code?
questions.answer: (Situation) Same Lambda code, three environments with different resource names. (Task) Deploy without code duplication or hardcoded resource names. (Action) Used Lambda environment variables — set TABLE_NAME and SNS_TOPIC_ARN as environment variables in each function's configuration. Code reads os.environ['TABLE_NAME'] instead of hardcoding 'Inventory'. Created three separate Lambda function versions or aliases (dev, staging, prod), each with different environment variable values pointing to environment-specific resources. (Result) Single codebase, three environments — changing from dev to prod is a configuration change, not a code change.

questions.question: Situation: Your Lambda function reads from DynamoDB Streams. One batch of 10 records keeps failing — maybe a malformed item. The function retries, fails, retries, fails. What happens to newer records?
questions.answer: (Situation) One failing batch is causing repeated retries. (Task) Understand the impact on stream processing. (Action) Explained DynamoDB Streams sharding — within a shard, records are processed in order. A persistently-failing batch blocks all newer records in that shard until it either succeeds or ages out of the 24-hour retention window. This can cause a significant processing backlog. Solution: configure a failure destination (SQS dead-letter queue or EventBridge) in the event source mapping, and set maxRetryAttempts or bisectBatchOnError to isolate the problematic record. (Result) With a DLQ configured, failed batches are sent to SQS for manual inspection while newer records continue processing normally.

questions.question: Situation: The CloudFormation template deployment fails with 'Requires capabilities: CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM'. What does this mean and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) CloudFormation stack creation fails with a capabilities error. (Task) Understand the error and deploy successfully. (Action) Explained that CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM is a required acknowledgment when a CloudFormation template creates IAM resources with custom names — it's a safety check requiring you to explicitly confirm that the template modifies IAM. Fixed by adding --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM to the CLI command, or checking the acknowledgment checkbox in the console wizard. (Result) Stack deployed successfully, creating the DynamoDB table, S3 bucket, and both IAM roles.

questions.question: Situation: You upload Springfield's inventory CSV. The dashboard shows Echo Dot, Echo Plus, Amazon Tap, Echo Look, Echo (2nd Gen) with correct counts, but Echo Show is missing. What's wrong?
questions.answer: (Situation) One row is missing from DynamoDB after upload. (Task) Find why Echo Show (count=0) didn't load. (Action) Checked CloudWatch logs for Load-Inventory — saw print statements for all 6 rows. Looked for exceptions after the Echo Show row. Checked the CSV directly — Echo Show has count=0. Considered: does the Lambda code skip rows with count=0? Reviewed the code — no, it writes all rows including zeros using put_item. Checked DynamoDB directly with a scan — Echo Show WAS there with Count=0. Dashboard may be filtering out zero-count items or there's a display issue. (Result) Echo Show was in DynamoDB with count=0 — it's the out-of-stock item that triggered the SNS alert. Dashboard behavior was expected.

questions.question: Compare Lambda's scaling behavior to EC2 Auto Scaling. When would you choose each?
questions.answer: Lambda scales automatically per invocation — each event gets its own container instance, up to the account's concurrency limit (default 1,000 concurrent executions per region). No configuration needed; it's instant and automatic. EC2 Auto Scaling scales at the instance level — it takes 1-5 minutes to launch a new instance, requires configuration of scaling policies, and is best for workloads that are long-running or require a persistent process. Choose Lambda when: workloads are event-driven, short-duration, highly variable, or rarely used. Choose EC2 when: workloads are long-running, require GPU/specific hardware, run continuous background processes, or need specialized OS configuration. For the inventory pipeline, Lambda is clearly superior — files arrive sporadically, processing takes seconds, and zero resources are needed between uploads.

questions.question: What architectural alternatives exist to overcome the API Gateway 29-second timeout limitation for long-running Lambda functions?
questions.answer: Several patterns address this: (1) Asynchronous pattern — API Gateway immediately returns a job ID, Lambda processes in the background, client polls another endpoint for results; (2) WebSocket API — maintains a persistent connection, Lambda sends results when ready (no 29-second limit for message delivery); (3) Step Functions — orchestrates long workflows outside API Gateway's timeout scope; (4) SQS decoupling — API Gateway writes to SQS, Lambda reads from SQS asynchronously (no synchronous timeout); (5) Streaming responses — some Lambda runtimes support response streaming for progressive output. Todd's recommendation: change the architecture, not the timeout — the 29-second API Gateway limit will never be raised.

questions.question: Explain how DynamoDB's composite primary key (partition key + sort key) enables the Inventory table to store multiple items per store.
questions.answer: A DynamoDB primary key can be just a partition key (simple) or a partition key + sort key (composite). With a composite key, the combination of both values must be unique — but the partition key alone can repeat. In the Inventory table: Store is the partition key, Item is the sort key. Berlin/Echo Dot and Berlin/Echo Show share the same partition key (Berlin) but have different sort keys, making them distinct items. This allows one table to hold inventory for all stores and all items without conflicts. DynamoDB uses the partition key to determine which physical partition stores the item — all Berlin items go to the same partition, enabling efficient queries like 'give me all items for Berlin.'

questions.question: How does the serverless architecture in this lab handle a scenario where 100 stores upload files simultaneously?
questions.answer: Lambda's automatic concurrency handles this natively. Each of the 100 S3 object creation events triggers a separate Lambda invocation. Lambda can run up to the account's concurrency limit (default 1,000 per region) simultaneously — 100 concurrent invocations is well within this. Each invocation independently downloads its file, reads it, and writes to DynamoDB. DynamoDB On-Demand handles the concurrent writes — since each store writes to different partition key values, there's no write contention. DynamoDB Streams picks up all 100 store updates and triggers Check-Stock for each. SNS publishes out-of-stock alerts for all affected stores simultaneously. The entire pipeline scales automatically with zero configuration changes — this is the architectural advantage of serverless.

questions.question: What is the Well-Architected Framework principle that justifies keeping Load-Inventory and Check-Stock as separate Lambda functions, and how does this apply to operational excellence?
questions.answer: The Operational Excellence pillar of the Well-Architected Framework emphasizes performing operations as code, making frequent, small, reversible changes, and anticipating failure. Separate functions embody this: each function can be deployed independently (small, reversible changes), failures are isolated (one function failing doesn't break the other), and each has clear, single-purpose logs (easier failure diagnosis). The Performance Efficiency pillar also applies — each function can be sized (memory, timeout) independently for its specific workload. The Reliability pillar benefits too — the DynamoDB Streams decoupling means if Check-Stock is temporarily down, the stream buffer preserves events for 24 hours, preventing alert loss during function updates or outages.
